---
title: "SQL tables"
---

`Phibble\Sql\SqlTable` is a table backed by a SQL query, like dbplyr's `tbl()`.
It implements the same `Table` contract as `DataFrame`. Verbs called with
[expressions](expr.qmd) are compiled into SQL, and no query runs until the
rows are needed. SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL are supported.

## Opening a table

`tbl($pdo, 'name')` opens a table or view. `tbl($pdo, 'SELECT ...', $bindings)`
starts from a query with positional (`?`) or named (`:name`) bindings. The
same tables can be opened with `SqlTable::table()` and `SqlTable::query()`.
`SqlTable::fromQuery($builder)` starts from a Laravel or Doctrine query builder,
and `SqlTable::fromSource($pdoSource)` from a `PdoSource`.

phibble reads the column names when the table is opened. It runs the query
itself when the rows are needed: `collect()` returns a `DataFrame`, and `toRows()`,
`nrow()`, iteration, and printing also run it.

`showQuery()` returns the SQL with `?` placeholders, and `bindings()` returns
their values in order.

{{< include examples/_sql-tbl.md >}}

Each verb wraps the previous query in a subquery, so each step's SQL stays
simple. Database planners usually flatten the nesting.

## What compiles to SQL

These verbs compile when their arguments are expressions or column names:
`select()`, `rename()`, `filter()`, `mutate()`, `arrange()`, `groupBy()`,
`summarize()`, `distinct()`, `slice()`, `head()`, and `join()`.

The compiled SQL keeps R's semantics:

- An aggregate returns NA when its group contains NA, unless `na_rm: true`.
  SQL aggregates skip NULL, so phibble adds a check on the count of non-NULL
  values.
- Cumulative functions return NA after the first NA.
- Ranks leave NA rows unranked.
- `isIn()` never returns NA.
- `/` returns a float, and division by zero gives NA.
- Groups in `summarize()` output are sorted, with NA last.

## When the table falls back to memory

Some arguments have no faithful SQL translation. A `SqlTable` then collects
the rows and runs the verb in memory, and the verb returns a `DataFrame`. The
values are then those `DataFrame` computes, apart from the
[known differences](#known-differences) below. The fallbacks are:

- any PHP closure,
- `round()`, because SQL's `ROUND` does not round half to even,
- `as_string()` and `as_bool()`,
- `paste()` and `paste0()` with arguments other than text literals, because SQL
  formats numbers differently from R,
- regular-expression patterns, except `str_detect()` in MySQL (which uses ICU,
  as stringr does). Patterns wrapped in `fixed()`, and plain patterns without
  regular-expression characters, are translated everywhere,
- `str_extract()`, `str_extract_all()`, `str_split()`, `str_split_i()`,
  `str_to_title()`, center `str_trunc()`, and `str_pad(side: 'both')`;
  `str_pad()` and `str_squish()` in SQLite; `str_to_upper()` and
  `str_to_lower()` in SQLite, whose `UPPER()` and `LOWER()` change only ASCII
  letters,
- parsing text to dates (`ymd()` and the others) on columns, `floor_date()`,
  `ceiling_date()`, `round_date()`, period arithmetic, `with_tz()`, and
  `force_tz()`, because the result type depends on the column type, which SQL
  tables do not track. Date parts (`year()` and the others), `wday()`, and
  `difftime()` are translated; a call on literals only, such as
  `ymd('2024-01-01')`, is evaluated once and passed as a value,
- functions of a PostgreSQL `time` or MySQL `TIME` column other than
  comparisons and `is_na()`, because SQL's time functions differ from
  lubridate's (MySQL's `HOUR()` of `25:00:00` is 25),
- any use of SQLite text that holds times, such as `7:30:00`, because it
  sorts and compares as text. SQLite columns are guessed as dates,
  datetimes, or times from their first 1000 rows when the table is opened,
- `sum()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `quantile()`, `sd()`, `var()`, and `iqr()`
  of date, datetime, and time columns, which keep R's types in memory,
- `first()`, `last()`, and `nth()` without a row order (from `arrange()` or
  `order_by:`), or with `default:` or `na_rm:`,
- `iqr()` outside PostgreSQL, `cumprod()`, and `consecutive_id()`,
- `sd()` and `var()` in SQLite, whose formula would lose precision,
- `str_trim()`, because R removes all Unicode white space and SQL `TRIM`
  removes spaces,
- nested aggregates such as `mean(x - mean(x))`, `summarize()` entries that
  are not one value per group, and `slice()` with negative positions,
- `median()` and `quantile()` outside PostgreSQL,
- `quantile()` without `na_rm: true`,
- `median()`, `quantile()`, and `n_distinct()` inside grouped `mutate()` or
  `filter()`, because SQL has no window form of them,
- `take()`, `eachGroup()`, `rowwise()`, `mutateGroups()` with closures, and
  `filterGroups()`,
- joins with `multiple`, `relationship`, or `unmatched` set, joins between
  different connections, full joins in MySQL, and full joins with NA matching in
  PostgreSQL.

{{< include examples/_sql-fallback.md >}}

SQLite compares by storage class, and it orders all text above all numbers.
A column declared without a type stores bound values as text, so
`col('x')->gt(0)` is true for every row of such a column. Declare column types
(`INTEGER`, `REAL`, `TEXT`) when creating SQLite tables that phibble will query.

## Known differences

These cases can differ from `DataFrame`, because the database cannot represent
R's result:

- MySQL has no infinity or NaN. Results that are `Inf`, `-Inf`, or `NaN` in
  R, such as `x / 0`, `log(0)`, or `mean()` of no values, are NA in MySQL.
  SQLite stores infinities but has no NaN, so `NaN` is NA there.
- Integer arithmetic beyond 64 bits fails in the database, where `DataFrame`
  switches to a double.
- Joins do not warn about unexpected many-to-many matches.
- Column names starting with `__phibble_` are reserved for the hidden columns
  that keep row order and window results.

Text compares in byte order and case-sensitively, as R does: phibble applies
`COLLATE "C"` in PostgreSQL and `utf8mb4_0900_bin` in MySQL to text columns
wherever values are compared, sorted, grouped, or joined.

## Window functions

Grouped `mutate()` and `filter()` compile aggregates and window functions to
`OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`. Window functions such as `lag()` and `cumsum()` need
a row order. SQL tables have none, so phibble numbers the rows of the source
query when the table is opened and keeps that number through every step.
Windows use the `order_by:` option where given, otherwise the order set by
`arrange()`, and otherwise the source order. The same order decides the order
of collected rows and breaks ties after `arrange()`, which is stable as in
dplyr. The source order is the order in which the database returns the
source query's rows. For a stored table, add `arrange()` to make it explicit.

{{< include examples/_sql-window.md >}}

## Joins

`join()` between two tables on the same PDO connection compiles to a SQL join.
The output columns follow `DataFrame::join()`: x's columns, then y's other columns,
with `.x` and `.y` suffixes on clashing names. NA keys match each other, as in
dplyr, through `IS` in SQLite, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` in PostgreSQL, and `<=>`
in MySQL. Pass `naMatches: false` for SQL's usual equality. The order of rows
from a SQL join is not defined, so call `arrange()` when it matters.

{{< include examples/_sql-join.md >}}
